objective: By the end of this lesson you can start a carbureted or fuel-injected engine with the checklist in cold, hot and night conditions, with battery or external power, and stop the start the moment a limit or warning sign appears.
why: As a commercial pilot you will start engines on busy ramps, in all weather, with passengers and line staff nearby. A good start protects people from the propeller, the engine from damage and the electrical system from a stuck starter.

prereading.what: Engine starting, starter and oil pressure limits, hand propping, ground running and chocks.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 2, 2-16 to 2-17

prereading.what: Carburetor and fuel injection systems, with the pros and cons of fuel injection for starting.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 7, 7-8 to 7-12

prereading.what: Starting system, starting circuit, and detonation during long ground runs.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 7, 7-18 to 7-19

prereading.what: Fuel pumps, the primer, and vapor lock.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 7, 7-25 to 7-26

prereading.what: Electrical system, ground power units, ammeter and loadmeter.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 7, 7-30 to 7-33

warmup: You land, refuel for 20 minutes on a 95 degree F afternoon, and the fuel-injected engine won't restart. Ten minutes later, on a cold morning, the same engine starts on the first try. What is different about the two starts?

key_terms.def: Electric switch that sends heavy current from the main bus to the starter motor only while the key is in START.
Plug on the airplane where a ground power unit (GPU) connects to supply electricity for starting.
Small pump that sprays fuel directly into the cylinders before a start. Lock it after use.
Electric fuel pump used for engine starting and as a backup if the engine-driven pump fails.
Part of a fuel injection system that replaces the carburetor and meters fuel by the mixture and throttle settings.
Fuel vapor or air in the fuel lines blocks fuel flow, making a start hard or impossible. Common on hot fuel-injected engines.
Crank no longer than 30 seconds, then let the starter cool at least 30 seconds to 1 minute, or as the POH says.
Gauge starting at zero that shows how much load is on the alternator or generator.
The disk the propeller sweeps. A spinning propeller is nearly invisible.
Hand-propping call meaning magnetos ON. Used because it sounds nothing like SWITCH OFF.

body.p: Most small airplanes use a direct-cranking electric starter. The system is a source of electricity, wiring, switches, solenoids and the starter motor. The starter engages the flywheel and turns the engine fast enough to start and keep running [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

bullets: Battery switch ON: the battery solenoid connects the battery to the main bus [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
The starter and the starter switch both draw from the main bus. The starter does not turn until the key in START energizes the starter solenoid [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Release the key from START and the solenoid removes power from the starter. A clutch in the starter drive lets the engine run faster than the starter [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Power for starting usually comes from the battery, but it can come from external power through an external power receptacle [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Some older airplanes have starters you engage with a lever instead of a key [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

callout.text: The spark does not come from this circuit. Magnetos make their own current, completely independent of the airplane's electrical system, and fire whenever the crankshaft turns [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]. The master switch powers everything except the ignition system [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

check.q: The key snaps back from START to BOTH. What two things keep the starter from being driven by the running engine?
check.a: The starter solenoid removes power from the starter motor, and a clutch in the starter drive lets the engine turn faster than the starter [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

chunks.title: Carbureted engines and the cold start

body.p: In a carburetor system, fuel and air are mixed in the carburetor before the mixture enters the intake manifold [[1:168|PHAK 7-8]]. Air flows through a venturi, a narrow throat. Its low pressure draws fuel from the float chamber out of the discharge nozzle into the airstream. The throttle valve controls how much fuel-air mixture reaches the cylinders [[1:168|PHAK 7-8]].

In cold weather there isn't enough heat to vaporize the fuel in the carburetor. That is why the primer helps: it draws fuel from the tanks and vaporizes it directly into the cylinders before the start [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

head: Cold start item
What the sources say
rows: Priming
Read the POH priming instructions to avoid overpriming [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]
Primer after use
Lock it. A loose knob can vibrate open and make the mixture too rich [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]
Engine heat
Preheat when temperatures approach and drop below freezing [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Oil
Use the right grade for the season [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Low oil temperature can mean wrong viscosity in cold weather [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]
Throttle after it fires
Open it gradually. Too much throttle after the engine fires is the main cause of backfiring [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Oil temperature
Rises slowly. After a cold start it may take several minutes or longer to move [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]

callout.text: Airplanes with a fuel-pump system (usually low-wing) also have an electric auxiliary pump for engine starting. High-wing airplanes are often gravity fed [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]. Your POH says when to use the pump during a start.

check.q: It is 20 degrees F. Why does a carbureted engine need the primer to start?
check.a: There is not enough heat to vaporize fuel in the carburetor. The primer vaporizes fuel directly into the cylinders [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

chunks.title: Fuel-injected engines: easy cold, hard hot

body.p: A fuel injection system sprays fuel directly into the cylinders, or just ahead of the intake valve [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]]. Many commercial training airplanes have one, so know it well.

bullets: Six basic parts: engine-driven fuel pump, fuel-air control unit, fuel manifold (distributor), discharge nozzles, auxiliary fuel pump, and fuel pressure/flow indicators [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].
The auxiliary fuel pump supplies fuel under pressure to the fuel-air control unit for starting. After the start, the engine-driven pump takes over [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].
The fuel-air control unit replaces the carburetor. It meters fuel by the mixture setting and sends it on at a rate set by the throttle [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].
The fuel manifold valve sends fuel to a discharge nozzle in each cylinder head [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

head: Fuel injection advantages
Fuel injection disadvantages
rows: Easier cold weather starts [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]
Difficulty starting a hot engine [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]
Better fuel flow and precise mixture control [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]
Vapor locks during ground operations on hot days [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]
Less evaporative icing [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]
Hard restarts after the engine quits from fuel starvation [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]

body.p: Vapor lock means fuel can't reach the cylinders, and a start may be difficult or impossible. On a hot fuel-injected engine, fuel can get so hot it vaporizes in the fuel line. Running a tank dry can also let air into the system and cause it [[24:389|AFH G-17]] [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]].

callout.text: Hot-start and flooded-start steps (mixture, throttle and boost pump settings) are different for every engine. The FAA handbooks don't give them, so learn your POH procedures before the checkride.

check.q: You stopped for fuel on a hot day, and now the fuel-injected engine won't start. What is a likely cause, and where do you find the fix?
check.a: Vapor lock: hot fuel vaporizes in the lines so fuel can't reach the cylinders [[24:389|AFH G-17]]. Hot starts are hard on fuel-injected engines [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. Use the POH hot-start procedure.

chunks.title: External power and the electrical system on start

body.p: Most aircraft have a 14- or 28-volt DC electrical system. The battery provides power for starting the engine, plus a limited supply if the alternator or generator fails [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

Some aircraft have a receptacle for a ground power unit (GPU), which provides electrical energy for starting. GPUs are very useful, especially for cold weather starts. Follow the manufacturer's recommendations for starting with a GPU [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. In the starting circuit, external power comes in through an external power relay to the main bus [[1:179|PHAK Figure 7-20]].

callout.text: AC 91-55A: accidents have happened shortly after takeoff because the starter relay (solenoid) stuck in the on position. The starter keeps running. That can overload the electrical system, overheat parts, and cause a complete electrical failure or destroy the starter and drive. Broken starter gears can also damage the engine [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 5]].

bullets: Know your airplane's normal readings, sounds and indicators after a start [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].
Warning signs of a starter that keeps running: low voltage, high ammeter or loadmeter reading, dimming lights, or excessive noise in the radios [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].
If you see them, shut the engine down. No further flight until the cause is found and repaired [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].
Some airplanes have a starter engaged warning light for this purpose [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

head: Gauge reading
Meaning
rows: Ammeter on the plus side
Charging rate of the battery [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Ammeter on the minus side
More current is drawn from the battery than is replaced [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Full-scale minus
Alternator or generator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Full-scale plus
Voltage regulator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Loadmeter
Percentage of the generating capacity in use, including battery charging [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]

callout.text: At idle right after start, a generator may not make enough current for the whole system, so the battery carries the load. An alternator makes enough current even at slow engine speeds [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

check.q: Right after start your radios whine loudly and the panel lights dim. What could be happening and what do you do?
check.a: The starter may still be running from a stuck starter relay. Shut down and don't fly until it is repaired [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].

chunks.title: Engine limits during and after start

body.p: Starters are electric motors that are not designed for continuous duty. Long, hard starts build up heat that damages the starter [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. The engine also has limits right after it fires, when oil has not yet reached every part.

head: Limit
Value or action
rows: Starter cranking
No more than 30 seconds, then cool at least 30 seconds to 1 minute. Some POHs ask for longer [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Smell of burning insulation
The cranking time may have been exceeded [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Repeated failed starts
Get advice from a qualified person to find the cause [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Oil pressure
At least the lower limit within 30 seconds in most conditions. If not, shut down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Rpm after start
POH value; in general 1,000 rpm, to let oil pressure rise and limit wear [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Warm-up rpm
Manufacturer's value, usually 1,000 to 1,300 rpm [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]

body.p: Most piston engines are air cooled and need forward speed to cool well, so the cooling system is weakest on the ground [[24:54|AFH 2-17]] [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]. Long ground runs with poor cylinder cooling can cause detonation [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].

bullets: Ground running: head into the wind, cowling installed, and watch the engine instruments at all times [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
Cowl flaps: keep them open on the ground. Don't close them to warm the engine [[24:54|AFH 2-17]] [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].
Constant-speed propeller: start with the propeller control in low pitch/high rpm. This reduces propeller load for easier starting and warm-up [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].
Manifold pressure gauge: with the engine stopped it shows ambient pressure; after the start it drops below ambient (for example, about 12 inches at idle) [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].

callout.text: 30 to crank, 30 to cool, 30 for oil. Then open cowls, nose into wind, prop forward.
Looking ahead to turbines: there, a hot start means the exhaust gas temperature went over its limit during the start [[1:183|PHAK 7-23]]. Don't confuse it with starting a hot piston engine.

check.q: You have cranked for 30 seconds with no start. What does the AFH say to do next?
check.a: Stop cranking and let the starter cool at least 30 seconds to 1 minute, or longer if the POH says so [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

body.p: Before start, the ramp around the airplane must be clear of persons, equipment and other hazards that could touch the airplane or the propeller. Check what is behind you, too: a propeller can throw objects fast enough to damage property and hurt people [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

bullets: Structures: don't point prop blast at an open hangar, parked cars or a fuel truck [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Surface: park where the propeller won't stir up gravel or dust. Chock the wheels and set the brakes [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

Other aircraft: powerful aircraft make exhaust blast or rotor downwash that can make a light airplane uncontrollable [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. In one case a small airplane 150 feet behind and to the side of an airliner got a wing and prop strike when the airliner powered up [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.4]].
Wind: for any ground running, point the nose into the wind for the best cooling [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
People: passengers move on the ramp only as you direct, with an escort if you can't supervise them [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

body.p: On a staffed ramp, line personnel may guide you with hand signals. What matters most is that everyone uses a suitable, agreed-upon set of signals [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

callout.text: At night the Emergency Stop signal is used for all stop indications [[24:52|AFH Figure 2-13]].

check.q: Name the four things the ACS says to consider when you position the airplane for start.
check.a: Structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property (ACS CA.II.C.S1).

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: start and after-start checks

body.p: Engines vary a lot, so the approved start checklist in your AFM/POH comes first [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Before engine start and Engine starting are both phases that need a prepared checklist [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. The steps below are the general safety items the AFH adds to any start.

bullets: 1. Before Engine Start checklist complete. Organize charts and items before you start [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
2. Constant-speed propeller: control forward to low pitch/high rpm [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]. Cowl flaps open [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
3. Clear the area all around and behind the airplane [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
4. Anti-collision lights ON. At night, position lights ON too [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
5. Brakes held firmly and one hand on the throttle, so the airplane can't lunge forward [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
6. Call "CLEAR" out the side window and wait for a response [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
7. Engage the starter. Release it as soon as the engine runs [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
8. Set the POH rpm (in general about 1,000 rpm) [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
9. Oil pressure: rising to at least the lower limit within 30 seconds [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
10. Ammeter, loadmeter or voltage: normal for your airplane, with no sign the starter is still running [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].
11. Listen and look for unusual sounds, vibration, smells or smoke. Any concern means shut down and investigate [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
12. Complete the After Start / Before Taxi checklist.

head: ACS element
What the examiner wants to see
rows: ACS CA.II.C.S1
Position the airplane properly considering structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property.
ACS CA.II.C.S2
Complete the appropriate checklist(s).

callout.text: Night start: scan the area with extra care, and you may turn off unneeded electrical equipment until after the start to save the battery [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
This Task has no number tolerances. At the commercial level the examiner expects you to run the checklist smoothly and explain why each step matters, without prompting.

check.q: After start, which two gauge checks come first, and why?
check.a: Oil pressure, which must rise within 30 seconds or you shut down, and the ammeter or loadmeter, which shows if the starter is still engaged [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

body.p: The propeller is nearly invisible when it spins. People have been seriously hurt and killed walking or reaching into the arc to remove chocks, reach the cabin, or walk toward the tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

bullets: Whenever you touch a propeller, assume the ignition is on. A faulty switch can sit at OFF and still let the engine start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

If the magneto ground wire breaks, the engine can start when the propeller is moved, even with the switch OFF. The only way to stop it is mixture to idle cutoff, then have an AMT check it [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].
After shutdown, turn the ignition switch OFF. With it ON, the engine can fire with the battery and master OFF [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].
To remove chocks with the engine running: throttle to idle, and approach only from behind the propeller, never from the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

body.p: Hand propping is hazardous even when done perfectly. If the airplane has a starter it should work; if not, call a certificated AMT. Hand propping is for airplanes built without a starter, done only by competent people per the AFM/POH [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

head: Hand-propping rule
Reason
rows: Two trained people. Someone who knows the controls sits in the pilot seat [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Brakes and switches are worked as directed
Firm footing; move the airplane if there is gravel, wet grass, grease, mud, oil, ice or snow [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
A slip can put the person into the blades
Face the blade, slightly less than one arm's length away [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
No leaning forward off balance
Push down with both palms, then step back [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Gripping fingers can pull you in on a kickback
Use CONTACT and SWITCH OFF [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Hard to confuse in noise or high wind
No start? Don't reposition the blade until the switch is verified OFF [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
The next pull could start it

callout.text: Never let a person unfamiliar with the controls sit in the pilot seat during hand propping. A runaway airplane is a real result of getting this wrong [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

check.q: A line worker needs to pull the chocks while your engine runs. How do you make it safe?
check.a: Throttle to idle, and the worker approaches only from behind the propeller, never from the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Starting from memory
Use the checklist; relying only on memory is complacency [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]
Cranking past 30 seconds on a hot engine
Stop, cool the starter, use the POH hot-start steps [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Overpriming or leaving the primer unlocked
Prime per the POH and lock it [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]
Big throttle burst on a cold engine
Open the throttle gradually [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Propeller control aft for start
Low pitch/high rpm for start [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]
Cowl flaps closed on the ground
Open on the ground [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Ignoring a high ammeter or dim lights after start
Shut down; suspect a stuck starter [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]]
Prop blast aimed at a hangar, or parked close behind a jet
Check behind and give jets ample distance [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.4]]

check.q: Which common error can damage a cold engine right after it fires?
check.a: Opening the throttle too fast. Excessive throttle after the engine fires is the main cause of backfiring [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

f1.caption: Figure 7-20. Typical starting circuit.
f1.alt: Wiring diagram. An external power plug feeds an external power relay, and a battery feeds a battery contactor (solenoid); both connect to an orange main bus. The ignition switch (OFF, L, R, B, S) energizes a starter contactor in the S position, which sends power to the starter motor. A red ALT/BAT master switch sits at lower left.

f2.caption: Figure 7-13. Fuel injection system.
f2.alt: Four-cylinder engine with a propeller on top. Blue fuel lines run from a fuel tank through an auxiliary fuel pump and an engine-driven fuel pump to a fuel-air control unit, then to a fuel manifold valve on top of the engine. Yellow fuel lines run from the manifold valve to each cylinder.

f3.caption: Figure 7-10. Float-type carburetor.
f3.alt: Cutaway of a carburetor. Air enters at the bottom air inlet, passes the discharge nozzle in the narrow venturi, and flows past the round throttle valve as fuel-air mixture. On the right, a green float in the float chamber controls the fuel level, with the fuel inlet, mixture needle and air bleed labeled.

f4.caption: Figure 7-35. Ammeter and loadmeter.
f4.alt: Two panel gauges. Left: a round ammeter with zero at the top center and a scale running from minus 60 on the left to plus 60 on the right, needle at zero. Right: a rectangular loadmeter marked 0, 30, 60 ALT AMPS with the needle at 30.

f5.caption: Figure 2-13. Standard hand signals used to assist pilots in managing a safe departure from the ramp to the taxiway or runway. Note that at night, the Emergency Stop signal is used for all stop indications.
f5.alt: Signalman in a red vest showing ramp signals: flagman, signalman's position, towing, stop, come ahead, emergency stop, cut engines, start engines, pull chocks, insert chocks, slow down, all clear, left turn, right turn, and night operation with lighted wands.

f6.caption: Figure 7-30. Gravity-feed and fuel-pump systems.
f6.alt: Two fuel system drawings. Top, gravity feed: left and right tanks with vent, selector valve, strainer, primer and carburetor. Bottom, fuel-pump system: tanks below a selector valve, strainer, primer, an electric pump and an engine-driven pump feeding the carburetor.

scenario.title: Dark, cold ramp with a weak battery
scenario.setup: You are flying two paying passengers out at 6:00 a.m. in January. It is 12 degrees F and dark. The fuel-injected airplane sat outside overnight, and yesterday the battery cranked slowly. The FBO offers a preheat and a GPU cart. Your passengers arrive while a line worker is pulling the GPU toward your airplane.

questions.q: Your passengers start walking toward the airplane on their own. What do you do?
questions.a: Brief them to move on the ramp only as you direct, and escort them if you can't supervise them [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Check the dark ramp with a flashlight before you board [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

questions.q: What should you do about the cold engine before you crank?
questions.a: Take the preheat: apply engine preheat when temperatures approach and drop below freezing, with the right oil grade for the season [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Fuel injection makes cold starts easier, but follow the POH start steps [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

questions.q: The line worker plugs in the GPU. Whose procedure do you follow, and how do you work with the line worker?
questions.a: Follow the manufacturer's GPU starting recommendations [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. Agree on hand signals first [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. When the cart is removed, keep the throttle at idle and the worker behind the propeller arc, never in front or to the side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

questions.q: The engine starts. Oil pressure reaches the bottom of the green at 25 seconds, but the oil temperature has barely moved after 5 minutes. Problem?
questions.a: No. Oil pressure came up within 30 seconds [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. After a cold start, oil temperature can take several minutes or longer to rise [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

questions.q: After the GPU is removed, the loadmeter stays very high and the panel lights look dim. What do you suspect and do?
questions.a: A stuck starter relay is possible: high loadmeter and dimming lights are warning signs. Compare to your known normal readings, shut down if they don't match, and don't fly until it is repaired [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]] [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

skills.do: Position the airplane properly considering structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property. The ACS gives no number tolerance. The examiner watches where your prop blast points, how you clear the area, and whether you call "CLEAR" and wait.
skills.practice: On every lesson, say your clearing scan out loud: front, both sides, behind. Before you start, name where the prop blast will go and what is behind it, check for gravel under the propeller, and look for jets or large aircraft nearby [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]] [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

skills.do: Complete the appropriate checklist(s): Before Engine Start, Engine Start (normal, cold, hot or external power as the conditions need), and After Start. Check oil pressure, rpm and the electrical gauges after start.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the POH start checklists, including the hot-start and GPU procedures, touching each control. In the airplane, use the checklist every time; never rely only on memory [[24:36|AFH 1-15]] [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

quiz.q: The battery switch is ON. Why doesn't the starter turn yet?
options: The starter solenoid is not energized until the key is in START
The alternator half of the master switch is OFF
The magnetos are still grounded
The starter clutch is disengaged until oil pressure rises
quiz.why: The starter draws from the main bus but will not operate until the starter switch in START energizes the starting solenoid [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

quiz.q: On a fuel-injected engine, what supplies fuel pressure to the fuel-air control unit for the start?
options: The engine-driven fuel pump
The auxiliary fuel pump
The primer
Gravity from the wing tanks
quiz.why: The auxiliary fuel pump supplies fuel under pressure for starting. After the start, the engine-driven pump takes over [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].

quiz.q: Which does the PHAK list as a disadvantage of fuel injection?
options: More carburetor icing
Harder cold weather starts
Difficulty starting a hot engine
Slower throttle response
quiz.why: Difficulty starting a hot engine is a listed disadvantage. Easier cold starts, less icing and faster throttle response are advantages [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

quiz.q: Why should the primer be locked after you use it?
options: So the auxiliary pump can build pressure
So it doesn't drain the battery
So fuel can't flow back to the tank
So it can't vibrate open and make the mixture too rich
quiz.why: A loose primer knob can vibrate out of position in flight and cause an excessively rich mixture [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

quiz.q: AC 91-55A warns about a starter relay that sticks on after start. What can it lead to?
options: Electrical overload and possibly total electrical failure
A magneto that won't turn off
Vapor lock in the fuel lines
A rich mixture at idle
quiz.why: A stuck starter relay keeps the starter running. That can overload the electrical system, overheat parts, and cause complete electrical failure or destroy the starter [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 5]].

quiz.q: After start, the ammeter shows a full-scale minus deflection. What does it indicate?
options: A voltage regulator malfunction
An alternator or generator malfunction
A normal charge after a long start
A starter stuck engaged
quiz.why: Full-scale minus means the alternator or generator has failed. Full-scale plus means a regulator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

quiz.q: Where should the propeller control be for starting an engine with a constant-speed propeller?
options: High pitch/low rpm, to protect the governor
Midrange, to warm the governor oil
Low pitch/high rpm, to reduce the propeller load
Any position; it doesn't matter on the ground
quiz.why: Start in low pitch/high rpm. It reduces propeller load, so the engine starts and warms up more easily [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].

quiz.q: How should cowl flaps be set while the engine runs on the ground?
options: Closed, to warm the engine faster
Half open
Closed until oil temperature is in the green
Full open
quiz.why: Keep cowl flaps full open on the ground for maximum airflow. Don't close them for warm-up [[24:54|AFH 2-17]] [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].

quiz.q: When hand propping, how does the person out front move the blade?
options: Pushes it down with both palms, then steps back
Grips it with the fingers and pulls down hard
Pulls it up from below with one hand
Leans in from more than an arm's length away
quiz.why: Push down with the palms and step back. Gripping with the fingers can pull you into the blades on a kickback, and standing too far away makes you lean off balance [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

takeaways: Use the POH checklist for every start: normal, cold, hot or with a GPU.
Cold carbureted engine: preheat, prime per the POH, lock the primer, open the throttle gently.
Fuel injection: easy cold starts, hard hot starts. Vapor lock is the usual hot-day problem.
Crank 30 seconds max, then cool 30 seconds to 1 minute. Oil pressure up within 30 seconds or shut down.
After start, watch for a stuck starter: high ammeter or loadmeter, low voltage, dim lights, radio noise.
On the ground: cowl flaps open, nose into wind, prop control forward.
Treat every propeller as live, and approach chocks only from behind the propeller.
cfi_notes: Have the student brief the POH hot-start, flooded-start and GPU procedures out loud before the checkride. The FAA handbooks don't cover them, and examiners like to ask "What if it floods?"
Teach the AC 91-55A warning signs and make the student state the airplane's normal after-start ammeter or loadmeter reading. Many pilots never look at it [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].
The AFH gives 1,000 rpm in general after start and usually 1,000 to 1,300 rpm for warm-up. Both are fine; the POH number wins [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
Pilots moving up from fixed-pitch trainers often start with the prop control aft or the cowl flaps closed. Build a start flow that checks both [[24:239|AFH 12-8]] [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
Clear up the word "hot start": on a piston engine it means starting a hot engine; on a turbine it means an over-temperature start [[1:183|PHAK 7-23]].
Ask: master OFF, key out, is the propeller safe? Teach the faulty switch and broken magneto ground wire hazards [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].
For S1, have the student say where the prop blast points and what is behind it before every start. Examiners watch positioning near hangars and jets.
gaps: No FAA source here describes a flooded engine or how to clear one. Teach the POH flooded-start procedure.
Hot-start, cold-start priming amounts and boost pump use during start differ by engine and are only in the POH.
The sources don't give GPU details (voltage match, connect and disconnect order, starting with a dead battery). Use the POH and FBO procedures.
There is no procedure here for an engine or induction fire during start; use the POH emergency checklist.
The ACS says "engine(s)"; this lesson covers single-engine airplanes only. The Skills elements have no number tolerances.

activities.title: Carburetor or fuel injection?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Fuel and air mix before the intake manifold
A float keeps the fuel level in a chamber
Fuel leaves a nozzle in the venturi throat
Ice forms easily near the throttle valve
A fuel-air control unit meters the fuel
A nozzle in each cylinder head sprays fuel
Easier cold weather starts are an advantage
Hard to restart hot on the ramp

activities.why: Carburetor: mixing before the manifold, float chamber, nozzle at the venturi, icing at the throttle valve [[1:168|PHAK 7-8]] [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. Fuel injection: control unit, nozzles in each cylinder head, easier cold starts, hard hot starts [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]] [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

activities.title: Read the ammeter
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.
activities.why: The ammeter's zero is in the center. Plus shows the battery charging rate; minus means more current is drawn from the battery than replaced. Full-scale minus means an alternator or generator malfunction; full-scale plus means a regulator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

activities.title: Starting numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You crank for the full 30 seconds with no start. Using the AFH minimum cool-down, how many seconds after you FIRST engaged the starter is the earliest you may crank again?
items.why: 30 seconds of cranking plus the minimum 30-second cool-down: 30 + 30 = 60 seconds [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

items.q: A hard start takes three 30-second cranking attempts, with the AFH maximum 1-minute cool-down between attempts. How many seconds pass from the first engagement to the end of the third attempt?
items.why: 3 cranks x 30 = 90 seconds, plus 2 cool-downs x 60 = 120 seconds. 90 + 120 = 210 seconds. After repeated failed starts, get help from a qualified person [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

items.q: Standard day, engine not running, field elevation 5,000 feet. About what should the manifold pressure gauge read, in inches of mercury?
items.why: With the engine stopped it reads ambient pressure. Pressure drops about 1 inch per 1,000 feet: 29.92 - 5 = 24.92 [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

items.q: Standard day, engine not running, field elevation 3,000 feet. About what should the manifold pressure gauge read, in inches of mercury?
items.why: About 1 inch per 1,000 feet below 29.92: 29.92 - 3 = 26.92. After the start it should drop below this value [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]] [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].

activities.title: Hot afternoon at a busy FBO
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a fuel-injected single with a constant-speed propeller and cowl flaps. It is 95 degrees F, and you have just refueled at a busy FBO ramp. Decide each step.

steps.s: Walking out, you see your tail points at an open hangar where mechanics are working, and there is loose gravel under the propeller.
options: Start now and taxi away quickly
Have the airplane moved to a clear, paved spot first
Start with low rpm so the blast stays small
Call CLEAR louder before you start
steps.why: Check what is behind you: prop blast can throw debris into people and property [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Park where the propeller won't stir up gravel or dust [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

steps.s: The airplane is moved. A business jet is starting its engines about 150 feet ahead and to one side, about to taxi past you.
options: Start and run up now, before it moves
Start and follow close behind it
Hold off until it has passed and you have ample distance
Start, but keep the brakes firmly set
steps.why: Jet blast can make a light airplane uncontrollable [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. A small airplane 150 feet behind and to the side of an airliner got a wing and prop strike, so give jets ample distance [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.4]].

steps.s: The jet is gone. The engine is hot, and your first 30-second crank doesn't start it.
options: Release the key, let the starter cool, and use the POH hot-start procedure
Keep cranking; it's almost running
Crank on the left magneto only
Ask a line worker to hand prop it
steps.why: Don't crank over 30 seconds; cool at least 30 seconds to 1 minute [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Hot fuel-injected engines are hard to start, so use the POH hot-start steps [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. If the airplane has a starter, it should work; hand propping is not the fix [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

steps.s: It starts. Oil pressure is in the green at 15 seconds, but the ammeter stays very high and the radio has a loud whine.
options: Normal after a hard start; taxi out
Turn off the radios and watch it
Raise rpm to help the alternator
Shut down; don't fly until it is fixed
steps.why: A continuous very high ammeter reading means the starter may still be engaged; shut down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. High ammeter and radio noise are AC 91-55A warning signs; no flight until repaired [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].

steps.s: After the repair, ATC says expect a 15-minute delay for your departure release. You will wait on the ramp with the engine running.
options: Close the cowl flaps to keep the engine warm
Cowl flaps open, nose into the wind, prop control forward, watch the gauges
Lean fully and set high rpm for cooling
Turn tailwind so the blast stays off the ramp
steps.why: Air-cooled engines cool poorly on the ground. Head into the wind, propeller in full low pitch, cowl flaps open, and monitor the engine instruments [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Long ground runs with poor cooling can cause detonation [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].

activities.title: True or false: lights and electrical checks
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A full-scale positive ammeter deflection after start points to a voltage regulator problem.
cards.why: True. Full-scale plus indicates a regulator malfunction; check the AFM/POH for the action [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

cards.s: Excessive noise in the radios right after start can mean the starter is still running.
cards.why: True. AC 91-55A lists radio noise with low voltage, high ammeter or loadmeter readings and dim lights [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].

cards.s: If the starter relay sticks on but the engine runs fine, you can fly and have it checked at your destination.
cards.why: False. Shut down; no further flight until the cause is found and repaired [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]].

cards.s: For a night start, the beacon alone is enough; position lights can wait until taxi.
cards.why: False. Anti-collision lights are on before every start, and at night the position lights should be on too [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

cards.s: Before a night start you may turn off unneeded electrical equipment to save the battery.
cards.why: True. This avoids excessive battery drain until the engine is started [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

cards.s: Once oil pressure is in the green, the electrical gauges can wait until the run-up.
cards.why: False. Check the ammeter right after start: a continuous very high current draw means the starter is still engaged and you shut down now [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

activities.title: Hand-propping calls in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Set fuel and engine controls for a normal start; check the magneto switch OFF
Out front: "FUEL ON, SWITCH OFF, THROTTLE CLOSED, BRAKES SET"
In the seat: check each item, then repeat the same words
Out front: pull the propeller through to prime, then call "BRAKES AND CONTACT"
In the seat: check brakes SET, magnetos ON, repeat "BRAKES AND CONTACT"
Push the blade down with both palms and step back
activities.why: This is the AFH hand-propping sequence and its voice commands [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

final_quiz.q: A line worker offers a GPU for your start on a 10 degree F morning. Where do you find how to start with it?
options: The FBO's fuel price sheet
Any GPU procedure from another airplane type
The manufacturer's recommendations in your AFM/POH
14 CFR Part 91
final_quiz.why: Follow the manufacturer's recommendations for engine starting using a GPU. GPUs are especially useful for cold weather starts [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

final_quiz.q: You shut down for 20 minutes on a 100 degree F day. Now your fuel-injected engine cranks but won't catch. Most likely cause?
options: Carburetor ice
Fuel vaporizing in the hot fuel lines
Oil too thick for the season
A fouled primer line
final_quiz.why: On fuel-injected engines, fuel can get so hot it vaporizes in the fuel line and can't reach the cylinders: vapor lock [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]] [[24:389|AFH G-17]]. Hot starts are a known fuel injection problem [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

final_quiz.q: On a ferry flight you ran a tank completely dry before switching tanks. Why can the engine now be hard to restart?
options: Air entered the fuel system and caused vapor lock
The magnetos lost their timing
The starter overheated from windmilling
The fuel selector jammed in OFF
final_quiz.why: Running a tank dry can let air into the fuel system and cause vapor lock, which makes the engine hard to restart [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]].

final_quiz.q: Standard day, field elevation 4,000 feet, engine not running. About what should the manifold pressure gauge read?
options: 29.92 inches
33.92 inches
21.92 inches
25.92 inches
final_quiz.why: A stopped engine's gauge shows ambient pressure, about 1 inch less per 1,000 feet: 29.92 - 4 = 25.92 inches [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

final_quiz.q: Which cranking plan follows the AFH guidance?
options: One 45-second crank, then rest
30 seconds of cranking, then 10 seconds of rest
Up to 30 seconds of cranking, then at least 30 seconds to 1 minute of rest
Short 20-second cranks back to back with no rest
final_quiz.why: Avoid continuous starter operation over 30 seconds without a cool-down of at least 30 seconds to 1 minute. Some POHs ask for longer [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: You turned the ignition OFF at shutdown, yet the engine fires when a mechanic turns the propeller. What could cause this?
options: The battery was left connected
A faulty switch or broken magneto ground wire
The primer was left unlocked
The alternator kept charging
final_quiz.why: Magnetos are turned off by grounding them. If the switch is faulty or the ground wire is broken, the engine can start with the switch OFF [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: That engine keeps running with the ignition switch OFF. How do you stop it?
options: Move the mixture to idle cutoff
Turn the master switch OFF
Pull the starter circuit breaker
Close the throttle fully
final_quiz.why: With a broken ground wire, the only way to stop the engine is mixture to idle cutoff. Then have an AMT check the system [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: An airliner is holding short ahead of you, and you plan to start and run up 150 feet behind and to its side. What does AC 90-66C suggest?
options: That distance is safe for light airplanes
Only rotor downwash is a hazard at that distance
It is safe if your brakes are set firmly
A small airplane there got a wing and prop strike; give more room
final_quiz.why: A small airplane doing a run-up 150 feet behind and to the side of an airliner had a wing and prop strike when the airliner powered up. Give yourself ample distance behind a jet [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.4]].

final_quiz.q: You are starting at night. Which lights should be on before you engage the starter?
options: Landing and taxi lights
Anti-collision and position lights
Landing light only
None, to save the battery
final_quiz.why: Anti-collision lights are on at all times before engine start; at night the position lights should be on too [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: A cold carbureted engine fires and runs roughly. What should you do with the throttle?
options: Pump it quickly to keep it running
Open it fully until it smooths out
Open it gradually and smoothly
Close it and re-prime
final_quiz.why: Excessive throttle after the engine fires is the main cause of backfiring. Gradual throttle opening on a cold engine reduces it [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

final_quiz.q: In winter your oil temperature stays unusually low long after start and in cruise. What might that point to?
options: A plugged oil cooler
A stuck starter relay
Too little oil in the sump
Improper oil viscosity for cold weather
final_quiz.why: Low oil temperature can signal improper oil viscosity in cold weather. High oil temperature points to things like a blocked cooler or low oil [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: During a turboprop checkout the instructor says, "Watch for a hot start." What does that mean on a turbine?
options: Exhaust gas temperature going over its limit during the start
Starting an engine that is still warm from flight
Starting on a day above 90 degrees F
Using a GPU instead of the battery
final_quiz.why: On a turbine, a hot start is when EGT exceeds the safe limit, from too much fuel or too little rpm [[1:183|PHAK 7-23]].

final_quiz.q: A vintage airplane with no starter must be hand propped on wet grass. What should you do?
options: Prop it carefully with a firm grip on the blade
Move the airplane to firm, clean footing first
Stand farther back so you can lean in
Have a passenger who has never flown hold the brakes
final_quiz.why: Wet grass can make the person slip into the blades; relocate unless firm footing is available. The seat occupant must know the controls, and you push with the palms from slightly less than an arm's length [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

final_quiz.q: The engine started and oil pressure is good. What warm-up rpm does the AFH say manufacturers usually specify?
options: 600 to 800 rpm
final_quiz.why: If oil pressure is indicated, set the manufacturer's warm-up rpm, which is usually between 1,000 and 1,300 rpm [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
